passage: I'm Alka. Bhupen and I were in the same batch, and lately his talk is all about how the process is rigged: referrals, polished English accents, seats that go by quota. I know some of it is true. Last month a panel asked where he learned his English, in a tone he did not like. But this week his laptop has stayed shut. Yesterday I mentioned two clerk openings and he said, "What's the point." Today, though, I found him in the library with a spoken English book, muttering the lines under his breath, and he sighed and said, "Unfair, yes. But I still need the job." Then he opened the form. I can't tell if he's bitter or planning. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did the panel ask Bhupen last month?
qa.a: The panel asked where he learned his English.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be feeling when he says "What's the point"?
qa.a: He may feel discouraged and bitter, though Alka can't tell for sure what is in his mind.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do with the parts of the process that really are unfair?
qa.a: He could name them honestly, then put effort into what he can control, like the spoken English practice and sending the applications.

qa.q: How does Alka see Bhupen's complaints?
qa.a: Alka accepts that some of it is true but worries the anger may stop his effort, and admits not being able to tell if he is bitter or planning.

grounding: Bhupen blames the system, which is partly true, and Alka watches him swing between shutting down and still applying.

passage:
Day 1: After the fourth rejection, Avni sat in the college library in Nagpur and listed the reasons: 'Quotas. Connections. They only want convent-school English.' Her classmate Akash, turned down by two of the same firms, nodded along. It felt good to be angry together.
Day 9: Avni skipped the mock interview session. 'What's the point, the system's rigged,' she told Akash. He went anyway.
Day 20: Akash got a call-back. Over chai he said the mock panel had helped him slow down. Avni went home and wrote two lists. On one: what really is unfair, like the firm that only visited English-medium colleges. On the other: what she could change, her nervous speed, her thin project list. She kept both. The next Tuesday she went to the mock session, and joined the speaking club too, not because her accent was wrong, but to feel steadier.

qa.q: What did Avni skip on Day 9?
qa.a: Avni skipped the mock interview session.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling on Day 9 when she skipped the session?
qa.a: Avni felt bitter and defeated, sure the system was rigged and effort was pointless.

qa.q: Why were Avni's two lists a wise step?
qa.a: They let her name what is truly unfair without making it the whole story, and pick things she could control, like her speed and projects.

qa.q: How might Akash's call-back have affected Avni?
qa.a: Seeing Akash get a call-back after the mock panel showed Avni that effort still counted, which helped her move.

grounding: Shows resentment at an unfair system turning into skipped effort, then Avni separating what is unfair from what she can control.

passage: Arohi, you say the interviews are rigged. Maybe some are. Let your Sahil-chacha tell you about my own year of that. I was twenty-one, from a Hindi-medium school in Gorakhpur, and in Delhi every panel seemed to smile at my accent. Four rejections. I decided it was all the system: English, contacts, surnames. Some of that was true; one panel really did ask only about my father's job. But for a whole year I applied nowhere. I sat at the paan shop complaining with two other boys. Then my friend Ghosh, rejected as often as me, got a job at a printing press by walking in with a folder of his work. I asked him how. He said, 'The unfair part isn't mine to fix today. My folder is.' I made a folder the next week. So be angry about what's unfair, Arohi. Then make your folder.

qa.a: Sahil went to a Hindi-medium school in Gorakhpur.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel during the year he stopped applying?
qa.a: Sahil felt bitter and resentful, blaming the whole system and giving up on effort.

qa.q: What turning point in the story got Sahil moving again?
qa.a: Seeing Ghosh get a job by walking in with a folder of work, and hearing that the folder, not the unfairness, was his to fix that day.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ghosh to keep trying after so many rejections?
qa.a: Ghosh likely felt the same unfairness but chose to focus on what he could control, which is why he walked in with a folder.

grounding: An uncle recalls blaming the system after rejections, some of it fairly, until a friend showed him how to name the unfairness and still control what he could.
